question:
A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of body aches and sore throat for 1 week. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He lives with his parents; they recently adopted a cat from an animal shelter. He is sexually active with one female partner, and they use condoms consistently. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 99/min, and blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The pharynx is red and swollen. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Leukocyte count 11,500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 48%
Band forms 2%
Basophils 0.5%
Eosinophils 1%
Lymphocytes 45%
Monocytes 3.5%
When the patient's serum is added to a sample of horse erythrocytes, the cells aggregate together. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "17-year-old boy with body aches and sore throat" -> "fever of 38.7°C (101.7°F)" -> "bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy" -> "red and swollen pharynx" -> "lymphocyte count of -> 45%

CHAIN: "17-year-old boy with symptoms of viral infection" -> "elevated lymphocyte count" -> "presence of heterophile antibodies" -> "indicates possible infectious mononucleosis" -> "most common cause is Epstein-Barr virus" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient presents with sore throat and fever" -> "examination reveals lymphadenopathy" -> "laboratory findings show lymphocytosis" -> "serum agglutination with horse erythrocytes" -> "consistent with heterophile antibody test" -> "most likely due to Epstein-Barr virus" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Symptoms of fever and sore throat" -> "lymphadenopathy and elevated lymphocytes" -> "positive reaction with horse erythrocytes" -> "indicates infectious mononucleosis" -> "most commonly associated with Epstein-Barr virus" -> 90%
analysis: The clinical presentation of the 17-year-old boy, including body aches, sore throat, fever, and bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. The laboratory findings show a lymphocytic predominance, which is characteristic of viral infections, particularly Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The key detail in the question is the aggregation of horse erythrocytes when the patient's serum is added, which indicates the presence of heterophile antibodies, commonly associated with EBV infection. Other options like Cytomegalovirus and Toxoplasma gondii can cause similar symptoms but are less likely to cause the specific heterophile antibody reaction. Therefore, the most likely causal pathogen is Epstein-Barr virus.
